item.title: Using AI Agents to Teach Robots Like Microduck to Walk in Simulation
item.abstract:
Teaching a robot to navigate an obstacle course requires more than a walking policy. It must perceive its surroundings, maintain balance, and adjust its actions when obstacles block the path ahead. Developing these capabilities connects several stages: creating assets and an environment, using physics simulation to model how the robot interacts with its environment, and training and evaluating policies in simulation. NVIDIA RTX Spark serves as a local development hub, supporting AI-assisted planning and policy validation. NVIDIA Isaac Lab provides the robot-learning framework for reinforcement learning in the cloud, while Newton models physical behavior, and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries generate simulated visual observations through RTX rendering. Trained policies return to RTX Spark for local evaluation in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . This post walks through the workflow using Microduck as a reference robot, with Hermes, NVIDIA Nemotron, and Astra assisting with planning and preparation. You’ll learn how to create a simulated obstacle course, train a navigation policy, and evaluate its behavior in simulation—a process you can adapt to your own robots and tasks. This establishes a foundation for physical deployment, where differences between simulation and real-world behavior require further refinement. Figure 1. Workflow overview 1. Create a plan of the obstacle course The workflow begins with a prompt describing the obstacle course and what Microduck must learn. On RTX Spark, Hermes and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt translate that prompt into a step-by-step project plan. The instructions establish the intended task, available resources, expected outputs, and the stages the agents should follow. Use the following example to structure your prompt: Build and test a simulated Microduck obstacle course with navigation and locomotion challenges. Make a photorealistic concept image and have Astra build and test it.
...
Workflow
Use Hermes and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt for preparation and Astra for asset creation and simulation.
...
1. Research and plan
Review official Microduck documentation and summarize capabilities, constraints, and unknowns. Define the course layout, obstacle dimensions, clearances, and intended route.
...
2. Generate the concept
Use a verified Microduck reference image to generate a photorealistic course concept. Check robot appearance, relative scale, and movement space; save prompts and provenance.
...
3. Identify assets
Extract unique reusable assets, group repeated instances, and select representative crops. Record dimensions, locations, and reference limitations; preserve original images.
...
4. Prepare the handoff
Package the plan, robot brief, concept, asset inventory, crops, and execution instructions. Verify required files, delegate to Astra, and wait for confirmed results.
...
5. Create and verify assets
Have Astra enhance references, model geometry in FreeCAD, and apply materials in Blender. Before simulation, verify every asset is completed or demonstrably blocked, with at least one usable model.
...
6. Assemble and test
Verify robot capabilities, assemble the course, and test navigation, challenges, and resets. Provide reproducible instructions and evidence; do not operate physical hardware.
... Local planning includes a brief review of Microduck’s repository and documentation . This review identifies the robot’s capabilities, resources for subsequent work, and details that still need verification. The resulting plan extends beyond asset creation: it outlines environment construction, robot preparation, simulation, training, validation, and deployment. The course needs to test both movement and perception. Microduck must learn to move around obstacles and through constrained spaces while maintaining balance. Use these requirements to guide the proposed layout and the objects needed to construct it. A local image-generation model produces a concept image of the course. Hermes and Nemotron then analyze the image and create an inventory of its visible, reusable assets. Each asset receives an identifier, a description of its visible features, and a cropped reference image. The inventory records where objects are cut off or obscured so that later stages can distinguish visible details from assumptions. Figure 2. Concept image and asset extraction from the obstacle course Hermes combines these outputs into a handoff package: the overall project plan, Microduck research and source links, the concept image, the asset inventory, cropped references, and instructions for the next stages. It then automatically delegates the work to Astra. The package gives Astra the broader project context and asset specifications needed to continue. Figure 3. Turning the task prompt into an environment plan 2. Create simulation assets Using the project plan and references from the previous stage, Astra creates the 3D assets needed for the course. Cropping objects from a larger concept image can result in small, low-resolution references. Before modeling, Astra uses cloud image editing to isolate the objects and produce clearer, higher-resolution images. Astra compares the enhanced references with the original crops, checking that silhouettes, proportions, colors, and distinctive features remain consistent. The enhanced images provide clearer modeling guidance, while the originals document what was visible in the concept image. Dimensions and hidden surfaces that cannot be established from the images are recorded as modeling assumptions. Astra directs FreeCAD to construct the base geometry and editable CAD structure, then uses Blender to add fine geometric details and materials. Both applications run locally through programmatic execution. The generated assets are saved as editable models and exported USD assets, with previews and output checks for review. Figure 4. FreeCAD modeling (left), Blender materials (middle), and the final asset (right), orchestrated by Astra You can also get assets from SimReady Central Library , a free and ungated library of more than 2,000 simulation-ready OpenUSD assets. Reusing them alongside newly generated objects reduces the asset preparation needed to assemble the obstacle course in Isaac Sim. The resulting assets become the building blocks of Microduck’s training environment in simulation. Figure 5. Obstacle-course assets created with Astra and assembled in Isaac Sim 3. Assemble the simulation environment Astra composes the obstacle course using the prepared assets in Isaac Sim. Isaac Sim provides access to Omniverse libraries’ rendering and sensor-simulation capabilities, while Newton models Microduck’s physical behavior, including movement and balance. A robot’s articulated structure and movement are defined in simulation through links, joints, and actuators. These elements establish the relationship between the policy’s actions and the simulated robot. Links represent connected bodies, joints constrain their relative motion, and actuators drive motion. Together, they model a robot interacting with its environment. AI agents can help configure these elements. Simulated sensor observations provide information about the obstacles ahead. As the robot attempts to walk, the simulation captures the consequences of its actions: whether it maintains its posture, makes progress through the course, or stumbles and falls. The result is a complete learning environment: a robot that can act, an obstacle course it can interact with, and a simulated environment that can generate feedback from those interactions. Reinforcement learning (RL) uses this feedback to train robot policies. Figure 6. The assembled environment in Isaac Sim 4. Train the perception and locomotion policy With Microduck and its environment ready, NVIDIA Isaac Lab provides the tools to train and evaluate robot policies at scale. This open-source framework runs many Microduck simulations at once, generating experience that an RL algorithm uses to improve its shared policy.

item.title: You.com Launches Inference Router: 12 Open-Weight Models With 99.9% Uptime SLA
item.abstract: You.com has launched Inference Router , a managed API for running open-weight models in production. The You.com Inference Router is an OpenAI-compatible service that routes requests across 12 live models. It bundles a 99.9% minimum uptime SLA and zero data retention (ZDR). It adds 100% US hosting and server-side web search. It is pay-as-you-go, with no platform fee. It is one API for many open-weight models. The endpoint is https://api.you.com , with OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible routes . Existing SDK code moves over by changing the base URL and key. You.com team frames the problem around stalled migrations. Dev teams test open-weight models on aggregators, then hit security review. Reviewers ask about ZDR, US hosting, access controls and DPAs. Dedicated providers clear those bars, but usually with a large commitment. Inference Router targets that gap. Every request goes first to You.com Inference Direct , the company’s own inference capacity. If it is down or full, the request fails over to a vetted partner. The official post names Parasail, Wafer, Alibaba Cloud, Meta and Inception, with Prime Intellect coming soon. All are 100% US-hosted and must meet ZDR rules. Failover does not change the bill. Each model has 1 published per-token price. You.com also offers spend caps per API key and daily usage views by model, cost and provider. Accounts run on SOC 2 compliant infrastructure, with a DPA on request. The ZDR policy states that prompts and outputs are processed in memory and not stored. It covers both model calls and web search requests. You.com keeps only operational metadata, such as token counts, timestamps and account IDs. Prompt hashes, de-identified text and disk-backed prompt caches are explicitly excluded. The models page lists 12 live models, all US-hosted. Prices are per 1M tokens (input / output): Muse Wonder, Muse Spark 1.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, Qwen3.8 Flash and MiniMax M3 round out the list. Developers declare a web_search or web_extract tool, and the router runs searches for the model. The docs show up to 20 results per search and a default of 30 search rounds. Responses return a web_results object with citations. Search runs on the same server as the model. You.com says internal tests show up to 15% lower latency. You.com reports a LiveNewsBench run of 1,329 questions, using Braintrust’s open-source search eval . These numbers are self-reported: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash costs about 77% less per question than Claude Sonnet 5.5. It trails by 2.26 points. Braintrust’s own August study used older models. There, DeepSeek V4 Flash with You.com search hit 80.66% at $0.0163 per question. Claude Sonnet 5 with built-in search scored 78.78% at $0.1148. You.com also cites joint work with NVIDIA and CoreWeave. Post-training Nemotron 3.5 Lightning with You.com search in the loop lifted BrowseComp from 36.97% to 45.45%. Tool calls fell by 30%. The clearest price win is versus Fireworks’ US-only tier. There, You.com is about 37% cheaper on Kimi K3 input. Check out the launch post , browse the model list and check the developer docs . item.title: Canva’s first AI image model plans designs before generating them
item.abstract: AI News Tech Canva’s first AI image model plans designs before generating them Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios. Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios. by Emma Roth Oct 22, 2026, 9:51 PM UTC If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Image: Canva Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Canva is diving even deeper into AI with the launch of an image generation model that competes directly with those from OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google. The model, called Canva Craft , uses a two-stage architecture that allows it to plan a design before generating an image, allowing for “greater precision, consistency and control,” according to an announcement on Thursday . Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios. In addition to generating social media posts and marketing content, it’s also supposed to create realistic scenes, digital art, environmental imagery, and more. The model’s two-stage system allows it to more accurately generate complex images that require legible text and precise object placement, according to Canva. Previous Next 1 / 5 An image generated by Canva Craft . Image: Canva The new AI model builds on Canva’s big push into AI. In April, Canva launched new prompt-based editing capabilities that allow you to create or make changes to a design by describing it. The design tool also brought layers to AI-generated images , which let you make changes to part of an image while leaving the rest untouched. Canva says it trained Craft on “millions of human-made templates” from the platform’s content library, which includes things like social media posts, presentations, infographics, and menus. The model is currently ranked fourth on Design Arena’s leaderboard for the best AI image generation models, a crowdsourced benchmark for AI designs. It sits behind OpenAI’s GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, GPT-Image-2.5 Flare, and GPT-Image-2. Canva notes that its AI model comes with “robust input and output moderation, privacy and safety controls, and reporting tools.” The company plans to allow AI agents to plug into Canva Craft through the open Model Context Protocol, and will also roll out more efficient Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast models in the future. Canva Craft is available now to all users globally. You can try it by navigating to the three-dot option on Canva’s left-hand menu and then selecting Dream Lab. item.title: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
item.abstract: Back to Articles LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape Enterprise Article Published October 23, 2026 Upvote 3 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Paper Encountering a new paper can change a research idea's trajectory. The researcher may discover that someone has already addressed their proposed contribution, or find an unresolved problem in the paper that inspires a new direction of inquiry. We call this process a literature-initiated pivot : a change in research direction prompted by reading prior work. It connects two activities that researchers often have to manage separately: developing an idea and deciding which literature to measure it against. With collaborators at the University of Pennsylvania, we developed LitPivot , a system that helps researchers navigate these pivots. Using papers retrieved through Asta Paper Finder , LitPivot organizes literature around the part of a proposal being edited, offers critiques supported by excerpts from selected studies, and suggests revisions that researchers can accept, edit, or reject. LitPivot is intended to be used for early-stage research ideation, but the idea could possibly extend to longer writing tasks (i.e., writing the introduction section of a paper). In a study with 17 researchers, domain experts rated research ideas developed with LitPivot as better grounded in the literature than those developed with a text editor and an AI chat tool. Participants also perceived their revised research ideas as more novel and useful, and reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature. LitPivot will be presented at UIST 2026 in Detroit. Read the paper here . Why pivoting is hard Research ideas evolve through engaging with the literature. In our analysis of meeting notes from four completed computer science research projects, we identified 21 literature-initiated pivots across all four projects. These fell into two types: differentiating an idea from existing work to establish an idea’s novelty, and aligning an idea with existing work to build on it. This project itself went through two pivots before we settled on its contributions. These changes can be difficult to navigate. In a formative study, five researchers developed proposals using a text editor and standard search tools. They struggled to develop their ideas while critically evaluating them against the literature. When a paper challenged an idea’s novelty, they wanted concrete suggestions for how to revise it, supported by prior work. These findings shaped LitPivot’s assessments, which pair literature-supported critiques with specific suggestions for revising the selected part of an idea. How LitPivot works In LitPivot, a researcher starts by writing a short proposal in an editor and enabling what we call facet highlighting , which segments an articulated idea into different facets (i.e., a problem, contribution, and evaluation). To check a proposed facet, the researcher clicks that segment in the draft. An adjacent panel groups related papers based on the selected facet (e.g., grouping papers by the evaluation methods they use when the evaluation facet is selected) and highlights the most relevant groups. The researcher selects papers, requests an assessment, and reviews a suggested revision alongside excerpts supporting the critique. The literature is then reranked based on relevance to the revised facet. In particular, LitPivot separates a research idea into its problem , proposed contribution , and evaluation plan . Each facet has its own set and relevance ranking of related literature. LitPivot groups retrieved papers around the facet being edited, letting the researcher choose which ones the system should use to assess the draft. Alongside scientific-writing environments such as Prism and agentic assistants such as Claude Code, LitPivot explores a new workflow for developing an early research idea: choosing literature to assess it against, using that evidence to revise it, and reconsidering which papers matter as the idea changes. Its paper groups and linked critiques make those steps explicit for each part of the proposal, while researchers control both the draft and the evidence used to assess it. For a problem statement, LitPivot looks for evidence that the problem exists and reasons it matters. To assess a proposed contribution, it compares what the selected papers have already addressed with the limitations and future work they describe, looking for remaining gaps. For an evaluation plan, it checks whether the proposed tests address the research question and how similar work has been evaluated. The system then suggests a rewrite with supporting quotes attached. Changing one facet of an idea can leave another out of date. LitPivot flags passages that may need revision, such as an evaluation plan that no longer adequately evaluates a revised contribution. Researchers can accept, edit, or reject suggestions, and request new papers or refresh the literature ranking as their proposal develops. Paraphrased example from one study participant. Our findings In our lab study, 17 researchers each developed one assigned idea with LitPivot and another with a baseline tool—a text editor and an AI tool for asking questions about selected papers. Both conditions used the same collection of papers. Two domain experts, unaware of which system had been used, rated the resulting proposals on a single criterion: how well they used relevant literature to support and justify the idea. Proposals developed with LitPivot received higher ratings. Participants in the same study also reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature and greater self-reported improvements in their ideas’ novelty and usefulness with LitPivot than with the baseline. Domain experts also reviewed the participants’ ideas and rated the ideas revised using LitPivot to be significantly better grounded in relevant literature. One participant in our lab study started with a proposal to generate consistent, factual synthetic medical notes. LitPivot identified consistency across multiple hospital visits as a potential gap in the selected literature. The participant reviewed abstracts and removed papers about single-visit notes. After another assessment, they narrowed the proposal to detecting contradictions across notes from multiple visits. The example shows how revising an idea and choosing the literature used to assess it can inform each other. In a follow-up study, five researchers used LitPivot on their own ongoing projects during 30-minute sessions. Participants used LitPivot across multiple project phases, not just at the beginning. Two used it to vet new ideas against the literature, while three used it to refine the framing of more mature ideas. One researcher highlighted how seeing parallel concepts from different domains helped them reframe their contribution. These studies suggest that LitPivot can support both early exploration and the refinement of an existing research direction. Supporting scientific discovery At Ai2, we’re developing AI to help researchers formulate testable ideas and examine the evidence behind them. Asta supports that effort through theory generation from published findings (Theorizer) , synthesis, and hypothesis generation and testing on data (AutoDiscovery) , while HARPA generates promising hypotheses informed by emerging research trends. Scideator lets researchers recombine elements of prior work into new ideas and assess their novelty, and IdeaSynth supports iterative refinement with feedback grounded in the literature. Our recent study, Old Ideas, Novel Problems , examines the limits of automated novelty evaluation, showing how small prompt changes can alter an AI judge’s verdict on the same ideas. LitPivot extends this line of work by making the choice of relevant literature part of the revision process.

item.title: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
item.abstract:
Back to Articles Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up Published October 23, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 8 +2 David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow In a previous post , we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do? The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself. Look up a model The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory. To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler ( neuronx-cc ) and of Transformers to look at. At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks. Run it yourself Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement : it loads the model with from_pretrained , sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron") . On a Trainium2 ( trn2 ) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container , install the packages, then run: python3 run.py No need for torchrun : the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded. A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version: hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache What "runs" means Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English. At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations. The results are a dataset Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions. Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly: import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet( "hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data" )
df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" ][[ "neuronx_cc" , "library" , "library_version" , "neuron_cores" , "result" ]] The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result. Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up .

item.title: 5 Free AI Coding Agents You Should Try in 2026
item.abstract: 5 Free AI Coding Agents You Should Try in 2026 Access powerful open-source and proprietary models through OpenCode Zen, Gemini’s free quota, Kilo Gateway, Cline Provider, and Charm Hyper without paying for API access upfront. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on October 23, 2026 in Programming AI coding agents are no longer just for companies or developers willing to pay for expensive APIs. Even without a credit card, you can now try capable agents powered by the latest open-source and proprietary models from Google and other AI labs. These agents can inspect repositories, edit files, run terminal commands, debug errors, execute tests, and work through complete coding tasks. That is one of the best parts of the current AI revolution: a lot of this technology is already accessible if you know which tools to use. The problem is that many coding agents still require a paid subscription or API key before you can properly try them. This guide focuses on tools that give you a practical way to experience agentic coding and test strong models without paying for API access upfront . Coding Agent Free Model Access Best For OpenCode OpenCode Zen free models Best overall Gemini CLI Gemini free quota Best free allowance Kilo Code Kilo Gateway free models Best variety of free models Cline Cline Provider free models Best for IDE users Crush Charm Hyper free tier Best terminal experience 1. OpenCode OpenCode is one of my favorite open-source coding agents, and I use it almost every day. It gives you a terminal-based coding environment where the agent can explore your repository, edit files, run commands, and handle multi-step development tasks. One of the main reasons I keep coming back to it is OpenCode Zen . If I want to test a newly released model, there is often a free option available through Zen, so I can try it directly inside my coding workflow without setting up another provider or paying for API credits. And these are not necessarily small or low-quality models. OpenCode regularly provides access to capable models for free, including variants from Muse Spark, Ling, NVIDIA Nemotron, and experimental or promotional releases. The exact free catalog changes over time, which also makes Zen a useful place to experiment with new models as they become available. You mainly need an OpenCode Zen account to get started with these free models. 2. Gemini CLI Gemini CLI is Google's open-source terminal coding agent. It can understand repositories, modify files, run shell commands, use tools, and work through multi-step coding tasks directly from your terminal. Google is probably one of the most generous model providers when it comes to free access. With Gemini CLI, you don't need to buy API credits or configure a separate model provider. You can simply install the CLI, sign in with an eligible Google account, and start using Google's latest Gemini models. There is an important limitation, though: free access is still rate- and quota-limited . It is great for testing, learning, and smaller coding tasks, but I wouldn't rely on the free tier for heavy, continuous development on large real-world projects. 3. Kilo Code Kilo Code started as a VS Code coding agent, but it has grown into a much broader ecosystem. You can now use it through VS Code, JetBrains, the CLI, and Kilo's cloud services , giving you much more flexibility in how you work. It also supports hundreds of models, so you are not locked into a single provider. The best part for me is its selection of free hosted models . Kilo regularly offers capable models at zero inference cost, and you can simply search for free in the model picker to see what is currently available. The exact selection changes as providers and promotions change, and some models may have upstream rate limits. Even better is Auto Free ( kilo-auto/free ) . Instead of choosing a model yourself, Kilo automatically routes your requests to one of the best free models currently available, with no credits required. That makes Kilo especially useful if you want to experiment with different modern coding models without constantly checking which free option is available. 4. Cline Cline is another coding agent I really like, especially if you prefer working directly inside your IDE. It can inspect your codebase, create and modify files, run terminal commands, check errors, run tests, and keep iterating on a task until it reaches a working result. Cline also gives you a lot of visibility into what the agent is doing, so you can review actions before allowing it to make important changes. What makes it interesting for free users is that Cline regularly provides free models through the Cline Provider . Once you sign in, you can open the model selector and look for models marked FREE . These options change over time and usually come with usage limits, but they are a great way to test new models, learn how Cline works, and experiment with agentic coding without immediately paying for API credits. 5. Crush Crush is one of my favorite options if you enjoy coding directly from the terminal. It is built by Charm, the team behind tools such as Bubble Tea and Gum, so the terminal experience is extremely polished. At the same time, it is a proper coding agent with support for file editing, terminal commands, LSP integration, MCP servers, and multi-step coding tasks. The best part is Charm Hyper , Crush's own model provider. Hyper has a free tier, so you can simply install Crush, select a Hyper model, sign in, and start coding without setting up API keys or buying credits. The free plan currently gives you 100 Hypercredits every month , which makes it useful for testing Crush and trying some of its coding-focused models for free. Which One Should You Use? If I were starting today, I would probably try OpenCode first . It gives you a really good balance of agent capabilities, model flexibility, and free access through OpenCode Zen. After that, it depends on how you like to work. Choose Gemini CLI if you want the easiest access to Google's Gemini models, Kilo Code if you want a large selection of free hosted models, Cline if you prefer working inside an IDE, and Crush if you want a polished terminal-first experience. Of course, free models come with limits. Quotas can change, promotional models may disappear, and they may not be enough for heavy work on large production repositories. But that is not really the point. You can now install a capable coding agent, connect it to a free hosted model, and start experimenting with agentic software development without paying upfront.
